Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 50, verses 6–11:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And there are no fissures in it﴾ have two interpretations:

The first: there are no cracks in it.

The second: there are no openings in it. This is what Ibn Isa said, except that the angel (al-Malik) has the gates of heaven opened for him at the time of ascent (al-'uruj).

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And the earth — We have spread it out﴾, meaning, We have extended it.

(p-342) ﴿And We have cast into it firm mountains﴾, meaning the firm, fixed mountains. Its singular is rasiyah. The poet said:

"Its root has settled beneath the earth, and it has risen high with a branch that cannot be reached, lofty toward the star."

﴿Of every beautiful kind﴾, meaning of every type.

﴿Pleasing﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: beautiful, derived from bahjah, which is beauty.

The second: delightful, derived from their saying, "This matter has delighted me (abhajanî)", meaning it gladdened me, because joy produces in the face a brightness and redness that makes it beautiful.

Al-Sha'bi said: "People are the plants of the earth; whoever enters Paradise is noble, and whoever enters the Fire is base."

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿As an insight﴾ have three interpretations:

The first: meaning an insight for the human being, said by Mujahid.

The second: blessings through which God made His servants see, said by Qatadah.

The third: meaning an indication and proof.

﴿And a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ has three interpretations:

The first: that al-munib is the sincere one, said by al-Suddi.

The second: that he is the one who repents to his Lord, said by Qatadah.

The third: that he is the one who returns and remembers, said by Ibn Bahr.

God has made this insight and reminder general, though the address is specific to every servant who turns back in repentance, because he benefits from it and is guided by it.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water﴾, meaning the rain, because by it plants and animals live.

﴿And We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾ has two interpretations here:

The first: that they are orchards, said by the majority.

The second: that they are trees, said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿And grain of the harvest﴾, meaning wheat, barley, and every grain that is harvested. When it is complete and ripe for harvest, it is called hasid. Al-A'sha said: (p-343)

"We are not like the people of Iyad in their land, where the grain's seed is watched until it is ready to be harvested."

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And tall date palms﴾ have two interpretations:

The first: that they are the tall ones, said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The poet said:

"O son of those whose virtue rose high over Qays and Fazarah."

That is, it grew tall over them.

The second: that they are those laden heavily with fruit, said by Ikrimah.

The poet said:

"When we left the house, it remained lofty, with palms laden with fruit in its vicinity."

﴿Layered clusters﴾, meaning piled up. It has three sayings:

The first: that al-nadid is what is piled up and layered, said by Ibn Abbas in the narration of Ikrimah from him.

The second: that it is what is strung together, which is also reported from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it is what stands upright and balanced, said by Ibn al-Had.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿As provision for the servants﴾, meaning what He sent down from the sky of blessed water, and what He brought forth from the earth by the water of plants, grain of the harvest, and layered clusters of dates.

﴿And We give life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence﴾. He made all of this a proof of resurrection and rising from two aspects:

The first: that if He created the first creation without a prior basis, then the second creation by restoring what has a basis is easier.

The second: that since His power has been witnessed in restoring what has died of crops and plants, restoring the people who have died is more fitting, because of the obligation that necessitates recompense.

.. ... ...

﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein.﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: it is a vein to which the heart is attached. This was said by al-Hasan.

And al-Asamm, and it is al-Waatin (the aorta).

Second: it is a vein in the throat. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

Third: what Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the vein of the neck, called the "cord of the shoulder." These are two veins, on the right and the left. It was called al-warid because it is the vein toward which what returns from the head is directed.

Regarding His saying ﴿and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ there are two interpretations:

One: "And We are nearer to him than the vein of his own that is part of him."

It may also bear a third meaning: "And We have more knowledge of what his soul whispers to him than the vein of his own that is part of his self, because it is a vein that mingles with the heart. So the knowledge of the Lord is nearer to him than the knowledge of the heart."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah said: "The two receivers are two angels who receive your deeds: one on your right, who records your good deeds, and the other on your left, who records your evil deeds."

Al-Hasan said: "Until, when you die, the scroll of your deeds is folded up, and it will be said to you on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner.﴾ By God, He is just toward you, Who made you the reckoner of your own self."

One: it is the one who sits (al-qa'idah), said by al-Mufaddal.

The second: the watcher who guards, said by Mujahid.

It is derived from al-qu'ud (sitting).

Al-Hasan said: "The guardians are four: two angels by day and two angels by night."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is a watcher ready.﴾ That is, he does not speak anything. It is derived from lafaza al-ta'am (he expelled food), which is expelling it from the mouth.

﴿but that with him is a watcher ready (raqib)⦆ Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: he who follows up on matters.

Second: he who guards, said by al-Suddi.

Third: he who witnesses, said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding ﴿'atid﴾ (ready) there are two interpretations:

One: he who is present and does not absent himself.

The second: the guardian who is prepared either for guarding or for testifying.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the agony of death has come in truth﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: what he sees at the moment of direct witnessing of the truth regarding what God had promised him.

The second: that the truth is death itself, and it is called "truth" either because it is deserved or because it transfers one to the abode of truth.

On this reading there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the sentence.

One: that it refers to the disbeliever, who was heedless of the consequences of his disbelief, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

First: that when he was in his mother's womb and was born, said by al-Suddi.

Second: when he was in the grave and was raised, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: that it is the time of the presentation on the Day of Resurrection, said by Mujahid.

Fourth: that it is the descent of revelation and the bearing of the message, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Zayd.

One: the insight of the heart, because through it one sees, from the evidences of thought and the fruits of reflection, what the eye sees of what is before it of persons and bodies. On this reading, regarding His saying ﴿sharp (hadid)⦆ there are two interpretations:

One: strong, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: perceptive, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: the tongue of the scale, said by al-Dahhak.

Third: what he will arrive at of reward or punishment, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿but that with him is a watcher ready (raqib)⦆ Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: he who follows up on matters.

Second: he who guards, said by al-Suddi.

Third: he who witnesses, said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding ﴿'atid﴾ (ready) there are two interpretations:

One: he who is present and does not absent himself.

The second: the guardian who is prepared either for guarding or for testifying.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the agony of death has come in truth﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: what he sees at the moment of direct witnessing of the truth regarding what God had promised him.

The second: that the truth is death itself, and it is called "truth" either because it is deserved or because it transfers one to the abode of truth.

On this reading there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the sentence.

Its meaning would be: "And the agony of truth has come with death." I found it so in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾ This may bear two meanings:

One: that he was avoiding death, so death came to him.

The second: that he was avoiding the truth, so the truth came to him at the moment of direct witnessing.

Regarding the meaning of al-tahayyud (avoiding) there are two interpretations:

One: it is fleeing, said by al-Dahhak.

(The second): it is deviating, said by al-Suddi.

From it is the verse of the poet:

*Indeed I said, when there was no escape from it for me, nor for men was there any escape from it.*

'Asim ibn Abi Bahdalah narrated from Abu Wa'il that 'A'ishah said in the presence of her father while he was dying:

*By your life, wealth does not avail a youth when the death-rattle comes upon him one day, and the chest is constricted by it.*

Abu Bakr then said: [Why did you not say as God said:] ﴿And the agony of death has come in truth; that is what you were trying to avoid.﴾

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ As for the driver (sa'iq), there are two statements:

One: it is an angel who drives him to the place of gathering, said by Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is a command from God that drives him to the place of reckoning, said by al-Dahhak.

As for the witness (shahid), there are four sayings:

First: it is an angel who testifies against him regarding his deeds. This is the saying of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and al-Hasan.

Second: it is the human being himself, who testifies against his own self regarding his deeds, narrated by Abu Salih.

(p-349) Third: it is the hands and feet, which testify against him regarding his deeds by themselves, said by Abu Hurayrah.

Then in the verse there are two statements:

One: that it is general, covering both the Muslim and the disbeliever. This is the view of the majority.

The second: that it is specific to the disbeliever, said by al-Dahhak.

One: that it refers to the disbeliever, who was heedless of the consequences of his disbelief, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it refers to the Prophet ﷺ, who was heedless of the message among the Quraysh in their jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

It may also bear a third meaning: "You were certainly, O human, heedless that every soul has with it a driver and a witness, because this is not known except through the divine texts."

First: that when he was in his mother's womb and was born, said by al-Suddi.

Second: when he was in the grave and was raised, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: that it is the time of the presentation on the Day of Resurrection, said by Mujahid.

Fourth: that it is the descent of revelation and the bearing of the message, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Zayd.

One: the insight of the heart, because through it one sees, from the evidences of thought and the fruits of reflection, what the eye sees of what is before it of persons and bodies. On this reading, regarding His saying ﴿sharp (hadid)⦆ there are two interpretations:

One: swift, like the swiftness of the "hadid" (the sharpness of iron).

The second: sound, like the soundness of cutting iron.

The second interpretation: that what is meant is the sight of the eye, which is the apparent meaning. On this reading, regarding His saying ﴿sharp⦆ there are two interpretations:

One: strong, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: perceptive, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

First: it witnesses the Hereafter, said by Qatadah.

Second: the tongue of the scale, said by al-Dahhak.

Third: what he will arrive at of reward or punishment, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: what he was commanded to do of obedience and warned against in disobedience, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: the deed that he used to do in the world, said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 50, verses 23–29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his companion said, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ As for "his companion" (qarin), there are three opinions:

First: that it is the angel who is a witness against him. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Second: that it is his companion from among the devils who was assigned to him. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: that it is his companion from among mankind. This was said by Ibn Zayd, according to the narration of Ibn Wahb from him.

As for His saying, ﴿This is what is ready with me﴾, there are two meanings:

One: "This is what I was charged with; I have brought it forth." This was said by Mujahid.

Second: "This is what I used to love and what loved me has come." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever.﴾ Regarding "cast" (alqiya), there are three opinions:

First: that the one commanded to cast every disbeliever into the Fire is two angels.

Second: it is permissible that it be one, and he is addressed with the dual form, as in the saying of the poet:

﴿Fa-in tazjurani ya Ibna Affana anzajir, wa-in tada'ani ahim 'arḍan mumannaʿan⟩

Third: that it comes out in the form of the dual of the verb, in the sense of your saying "cast, cast" and "stop, stop", as an emphasis of the command.

And "al-kaffar" (with a fatha on the kaf) is more intensive in emphasis than "al-kafir."

It admits two meanings:

One: that it is the disbeliever who disbelieved in God and did not obey Him, and disbelieved in His blessings and did not give thanks for them.

Second: that it is the one who disbelieved in himself and caused others to disbelieve through his misguidance.

As for "ʿanid" (stubborn), there are five aspects:

First: that it is one who opposes the truth. This was said by some of the later scholars.

Second: that it is one who turns away from obedience. This was said by Qatadah.

Third: that it is the denier who is defiant. This was said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: that it is the one who opposes. This was said by al-Suddi.

Fifth: that it is the one who is self-satisfied with what he has and persists in acting upon it. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

As for "ʿanid" (opposing), there are two meanings:

One: that it is the one who is made aware of the truth and then denies it.

Second: that it is the one who is called to the truth and refuses it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Hinderer of good﴾. In it there are three aspects:

First: that he withheld the obligatory zakah. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: that "the good" is all wealth, and withholding it means restricting it from spending in obedience to God. This was said by some of the later scholars.

Third: that it is to be understood as general of good, in speech and action.

﴿Transgressor, doubter﴾. Regarding "murib" (doubter), there are three aspects:

First: that it is one who doubts God. This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: that it is one who doubts the Resurrection. This was said by Qatadah.

Third: that it is the one who is suspected.

Third: they traveled through the lands and went around them. This was said by Qatadah, and from it comes the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I have roamed the horizons until I was content, from the spoils, with returning."*

Fourth: they made roads and pathways in them. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

It may also mean a fifth: the construction of fortresses and castles.

﴿Is there any escape?﴾ has three interpretations:

First: Is there anyone who can escape death? This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Second: Is there any place of refuge? Ma'mar reported from Qatadah: the enemies of Allah sought refuge, but they found the command of Allah reaching them.

Third: Is there any protector? Sa'id reported from Qatadah: the wicked sought refuge, but they found the command of Allah to be unassailable.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ has two interpretations:

One: for whoever has intellect. This was said by Mujahid, because the heart is the seat of the intellect.

(p. 356) Second: for whoever has life and a distinguishing self (*nafs mumayyizah*). The living self is expressed by "heart" because it is its homeland and the source of its life.

As Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Has your love for me deceived you, that it would kill me, and that whatever you command the heart, it will do?"*

﴿Or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ has three interpretations:

First: he gives ear to what is absent from him through reports, and he is a witness to what he sees in person.

Second: its meaning is that he hears what Allah has revealed of the Books, while he is a witness to its authenticity.

Third: he hears what he is warned of, of reward and punishment, and he is a witness against himself regarding what he has done of obedience or disobedience.

There are three opinions regarding the verse:

First: it refers to all the People of the Books. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: it refers only to the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: it refers only to the people of the Qur'an. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Abu Salih.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And no fatigue touched Us﴾. *Lughub* means weariness and exhaustion.

The rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

*"When the driver urges on the camels that are wearied, and the shade puts on the sock (of the shadow stretching out)."*

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: this verse was revealed concerning the Jews of Medina. They claimed that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, the first of which was Sunday and the last Friday, and that He rested on Saturday; for this reason they made it a day of rest. Allah refuted them in this claim.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾. This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), in which he was commanded to be patient over what the polytheists say, whether it is denial or threat.

﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾, the verse.

Although this is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), it is general to him and to his community.

Regarding this glorification there are two interpretations:

One: it is glorifying Him verbally, declaring Him free of imperfection, before the rising of the sun and before its setting. This was said by Abu al-Ahwas.

(p. 357) Second: it refers to prayer, and the meaning is: pray by the command of your Lord before the rising of the sun, meaning the dawn prayer, and before the setting, meaning the afternoon prayer. This was said by Abu Salih, and Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah narrated it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And during the night glorify Him﴾ has four interpretations:

First: it is glorifying Allah, the Exalted, verbally during the night. This was said by Abu al-Ahwas.

Second: it refers to the night prayer. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: it refers to the two rak'ahs of the dawn. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: it refers to the late night ('isha') prayer. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Then He said: ﴿and after the prostrations﴾, which has three interpretations:

First: it is glorification after the prayers. This was said by Abu al-Ahwas.

Second: it refers to the voluntary prayers after the obligatory ones. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Third: it refers to two rak'ahs after the maghrib prayer. This was said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn 'Abbas narrated, saying: "I spent a night with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he prayed two rak'ahs before dawn, then went out to the prayer and said: (O Ibn 'Abbas, two rak'ahs before dawn are the *adbar al-nujum* (after the stars), and two rak'ahs after the maghrib are *adbar al-sujud* (after the prostrations))."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 50, verses 41–45:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And listen on the day the caller calls from a near place﴾. This cry by which the caller calls from a near place is the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya), by which resurrection occurs, to the land of the gathering (al-mahshar).

It may also bear another meaning: that it is His call in the gathering for the presentation (al-ard) and the reckoning (al-hisab).

As for His words ﴿from a near place﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: everyone near and far will hear it. This was said by Ibn Juraij.

The second: the cry comes from a near place.

Qatada said: "We used to be told that it will call out from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), from the Rock, which is the middle of the earth: 'O you decayed bones, arise for the judgment of the decision and for what has been prepared of recompense.'"

We were also told that Ka'b said: "It is the nearest part of the earth to the heaven, by eighteen miles."

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿On the day they hear the cry in truth﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

The first: meaning with the word of truth.

The second: with the resurrection, which is true.

﴿That is the day of coming forth﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

The first: the coming forth from the graves.

The second: that "coming forth" (al-khuruj) is among the names of the Resurrection.

al-'Ajjaj said:

"There is no day named 'the coming forth' greater than the day that shakes it with a mighty shaking."

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿We know best what they say﴾. This may bear two meanings:

The first: We know best what they will answer you with, of affirmation or denial.

The second: what they conceal of faith or hypocrisy.

﴿And you are not over them a compeller (jabbar)﴾. There are three interpretations of this:

The first: meaning a lord (rabb). This was said by al-Dahhak, because the Jabbar is God, Exalted is His authority.

(p-359) The second: one who is arrogantly domineering over them, one who dominates. This was said by Mujahid.

For this reason every domineering person is called a jabbar.

The poet said:

"We, when the jabbar turned his cheek away in arrogance, we would straighten him from his arrogance until he stood upright."

And it is a blameworthy attribute when it describes created beings.

The third: that you do not compel them to Islam, from their saying "I compelled him to the matter" when you overpower him to a matter. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning (wa'id)﴾. The wa'id is the punishment, and the wa'd is the reward.

The poet said:

"Even if I threaten him or promise him, I will break my threat and fulfill my promise."

Qatada said: "O God, make us among those who fear Your warning and hope for Your promise."

It is also narrated that it was said: "O Messenger of God, if only you had warned us," and then this was revealed: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾.
